content:
U.S. Ambassador Eric Meyer today presented a master’s degree from the U.S. Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) to Lieutenant Commander Piyumi Kathriarachchi of the Sri Lanka Navy at the American Center Colombo. The ceremony was also attended by Rear Admiral Rohan Joseph, Director General of Training, and Commander C.R.P. Walakuluge, Director of Media, Sri Lanka Navy.

“Lieutenant Commander Kathriarachchi’s achievements reflect both her exceptional dedication and the value of world-class American military education. Through U.S.-funded training, she has gained knowledge and skills that she is now bringing home to strengthen Sri Lanka’s Navy. Her success demonstrates how investing in the professional development of our partners strengthens our defense cooperation and contributes to a safer, more secure Indian Ocean region,” said U.S. Ambassador Eric Meyer.

LCDR Kathriarachchi graduated near the top of her class at the U.S. Naval Postgraduate School (NPS), a graduate university in Monterey, California, that prepares military and defense professionals for leadership roles.

She completed the Defense Logistics Management program with honors, earning a 3.98 grade point average (GPA) out of a possible 4.0—nearly a perfect score. She also received the NPS Outstanding Thesis Award and the Kiwanis Club of Monterey Outstanding International Student Award, which the club gives to only two NPS international students each year.

Her studies were funded by the U.S. International Military Education and Training (IMET) program, which helps Sri Lankan military personnel develop skills and expertise they can bring home to strengthen their services and deepen defense cooperation between the United States and Sri Lanka.

LCDR Kathriarachchi’s award-winning research on spare parts procurement challenges facing the Sri Lanka Navy demonstrates how U.S. military education equips Sri Lankan officers with practical expertise they can apply at home, strengthening naval readiness and our bilateral defense partnership.

Reflecting on her studies in the United States, she said, “My time in the United States gave me new tools to tackle real challenges facing our Navy. I look forward to putting that knowledge to work in service of Sri Lanka and hope my experience encourages other young Sri Lankans to pursue opportunities that can make a difference for our country.”

A graduate of Taxila Central College in Horana, LCDR Kathriarachchi has a history of breaking barriers, becoming the first female midshipman in Sri Lanka Navy history to receive the prestigious Sword of Honour in 2013.

Minister orders independent probe into death of man in Homagama Police custody

Public Security and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Ananda Wijepala has instructed Inspector General of Police (IGP) Priyantha Weerasuriya to conduct an urgent and independent investigation into the reported death of a person who was in the custody of the Homagama Police.

The Minister has also instructed the IGP to take further legal action based on the findings of the post-mortem examination and the investigation into the incident.

The Minister emphasised that police officers have a responsibility to ensure the safety of individuals taken into custody and to protect their human dignity.

summary_en: ලාෆ්ස් ගෑස් පීඑල්සී සිය පූර්ණ අනුබද්ධිත සමාගමක් වන LAUGFS Terminals Limited සම්බන්ධයෙන් උපායමාර්ගික විකල්ප පිළිබඳව, ඒ සම්බන්ධයෙන් උනන්දුවක් දක්වන පාර්ශ්වයන් සමඟ මූලික සහ විධිමත් නොවන මට්ටමේ සාකච්ඡාවල නිරත වන බව සිය කොටස් හිමියන්ට සහ කොළඹ කොටස් වෙළෙඳපොළ වෙත නිල වශයෙන් දැනුම් දී සිටී. මෙම සාකච්ඡාවලදී සලකා බලනු ලබන විකල්ප අතරට වාණිජමය සහයෝගීතාවයන්, බාහිර ආයෝජන ලබා ගැනීම සහ LAUGFS Terminals Limited හි ලාෆ්ස් ගෑස් පීඑල්සී සතු කොටස් හිමිකාරීත්වයේ කොටසක් හෝ සම්පූර්ණයෙන්ම විකිණීම ඇතුළත් වේ. කෙසේ වෙතත්, කිසිදු ගනුදෙනුවක ව්‍යුහය හෝ කොන්දේසි පිළිබඳව මෙතෙක් එකඟතාවයකට පැමිණ නොමැති අතර, කිසිදු අවසන් ගනුදෙනු ගිවිසුමකට ද එළඹ නොමැති බව සමාගම පෙන්වා දෙයි. මෙම මූලික සාකච්ඡා සාර්ථක ගනුදෙනුවකින් කෙළවර වේද යන්න පිළිබඳව ස්ථිරභාවයක් නොමැති බැවින්, මෙම අදියරේදී සිදුවිය හැකි මූල්‍යමය බලපෑම තීරණය කළ නොහැකි බව ද සඳහන් කර ඇත. මේ සම්බන්ධයෙන් ඉදිරියේදී සිදුවන යම් සැලකිය යුතු වර්ධනයක් පිළිබඳව වහාම අනාවරණය කිරීමට කටයුතු කරන බව ලාෆ්ස් ගෑස් පීඑල්සී සමාගම කොළඹ කොටස් වෙළෙඳපොළ වෙත වැඩිදුරටත් දන්වා සිටී. LAUGFS Terminals Limited සමාගම හම්බන්තොට ජාත්‍යන්තර වරාය පරිශ්‍රයේ පිහිටි මෙට්‍රික් ටොන් 30,000 ක ධාරිතාවයකින් යුත් LPG (ද්‍රවීකෘත පෙට්‍රෝලියම් ගෑස්) පර්යන්තයේ අයිතිය දරනු ලබන අතර එහි මෙහෙයුම් කටයුතු සිදුකරනු ලබයි.
summary_si: මෙම පුවත Daily FT වෙබ් අඩවියෙන් ලබා ගන්නා ලදී. ලාෆ්ස් ගෑස් පීඑල්සී සිය පූර්ණ අනුබද්ධිත සමාගමක් වන LAUGFS Terminals Limited සම්බන්ධයෙන් උපායමාර්ගික විකල්ප පිළිබඳව, ඒ සම්බන්ධයෙන් උනන්දුවක් දක්වන පාර්ශ්වයන් සමඟ මූලික සහ විධිමත් නොවන මට්ටමේ සාකච්ඡාවල නිරත වන බව සිය කොටස් හිමියන්ට සහ කොළඹ කොටස් වෙළෙඳපොළ වෙත නිල වශයෙන් දැනුම් දී සිටී. මෙම සාකච්ඡාවලදී සලකා බලනු ලබන විකල්ප අතරට වාණිජමය සහයෝගීතාවයන්, බාහිර ආයෝජන ලබා ගැනීම සහ LAUGFS Terminals Limited හි ලාෆ්ස් ගෑස් පීඑල්සී සතු කොටස් හිමිකාරීත්වයේ කොටසක් හෝ සම්පූර්ණයෙන්ම විකිණීම ඇතුළත් වේ. කෙසේ වෙතත්, කිසිදු ගනුදෙනුවක ව්‍යුහය හෝ කොන්දේසි පිළිබඳව මෙතෙක් එකඟතාවයකට පැමිණ නොමැති අතර, කිසිදු අවසන් ගනුදෙනු ගිවිසුමකට ද එළඹ නොමැති බව සමාගම පෙන්වා දෙයි. මෙම මූලික සාකච්ඡා සාර්ථක ගනුදෙනුවකින් කෙළවර වේද යන්න පිළිබඳව ස්ථිරභාවයක් නොමැති බැවින්, මෙම අදියරේදී සිදුවිය හැකි මූල්‍යමය බලපෑම තීරණය කළ නොහැකි බව ද සඳහන් කර ඇත. මේ සම්බන්ධයෙන් ඉදිරියේදී සිදුවන යම් සැලකිය යුතු වර්ධනයක් පිළිබඳව වහාම අනාවරණය කිරීමට කටයුතු කරන බව ලාෆ්ස් ගෑස් පීඑල්සී සමාගම කොළඹ කොටස් වෙළෙඳපොළ වෙත වැඩිදුරටත් දන්වා සිටී. LAUGFS Terminals Limited සමාගම හම්බන්තොට ජාත්‍යන්තර වරාය පරිශ්‍රයේ පිහිටි මෙට්‍රික් ටොන් 30,000 ක ධාරිතාවයකින් යුත් LPG (ද්‍රවීකෘත පෙට්‍රෝලියම් ගෑස්) පර්යන්තයේ අයිතිය දරනු ලබන අතර එහි මෙහෙයුම් කටයුතු සිදුකරනු ලබයි.
content: ලාෆ්ස් ගෑස් පීඑල්සී සිය පූර්ණ අනුබද්ධිත සමාගමක් වන LAUGFS Terminals Limited සම්බන්ධයෙන් උපායමාර්ගික විකල්ප පිළිබඳව, ඒ සම්බන්ධයෙන් උනන්දුවක් දක්වන පාර්ශ්වයන් සමඟ මූලික සහ විධිමත් නොවන මට්ටමේ සාකච්ඡාවල නිරත වන බව සිය කොටස් හිමියන්ට සහ කොළඹ කොටස් වෙළෙඳපොළ වෙත නිල වශයෙන් දැනුම් දී සිටී. මෙම සාකච්ඡාවලදී සලකා බලනු ලබන විකල්ප අතරට වාණිජමය සහයෝගීතාවයන්, බාහිර ආයෝජන ලබා ගැනීම සහ LAUGFS Terminals Limited හි ලාෆ්ස් ගෑස් පීඑල්සී සතු කොටස් හිමිකාරීත්වයේ කොටසක් හෝ සම්පූර්ණයෙන්ම විකිණීම ඇතුළත් වේ. කෙසේ වෙතත්, කිසිදු ගනුදෙනුවක ව්‍යුහය හෝ කොන්දේසි පිළිබඳව මෙතෙක් එකඟතාවයකට පැමිණ නොමැති අතර, කිසිදු අවසන් ගනුදෙනු ගිවිසුමකට ද එළඹ නොමැති බව සමාගම පෙන්වා දෙයි. මෙම මූලික සාකච්ඡා සාර්ථක ගනුදෙනුවකින් කෙළවර වේද යන්න පිළිබඳව ස්ථිරභාවයක් නොමැති බැවින්, මෙම අදියරේදී සිදුවිය හැකි මූල්‍යමය බලපෑම තීරණය කළ නොහැකි බව ද සඳහන් කර ඇත. මේ සම්බන්ධයෙන් ඉදිරියේදී සිදුවන යම් සැලකිය යුතු වර්ධනයක් පිළිබඳව වහාම අනාවරණය කිරීමට කටයුතු කරන බව ලාෆ්ස් ගෑස් පීඑල්සී සමාගම කොළඹ කොටස් වෙළෙඳපොළ වෙත වැඩිදුරටත් දන්වා සිටී. LAUGFS Terminals Limited සමාගම හම්බන්තොට ජාත්‍යන්තර වරාය පරිශ්‍රයේ පිහිටි මෙට්‍රික් ටොන් 30,000 ක ධාරිතාවයකින් යුත් LPG (ද්‍රවීකෘත පෙට්‍රෝලියම් ගෑස්) පර්යන්තයේ අයිතිය දරනු ලබන අතර එහි මෙහෙයුම් කටයුතු සිදුකරනු ලබයි. content: Three (3) ships belonging to the Indian Navy’s First Training Squadron (1TS), INS Tir, INS Sujata and ICGS Sarathi, arrived in Sri Lanka today, 26 October 2026, on a formal visit. The visiting ships were welcomed by the Sri Lanka Navy in accordance with time-honoured naval traditions. A total of 135 officer under-trainees are participating in the visit across the three vessels. INS Tir, a Training Ship of 107m in length, is commanded by Captain Tijo K Joseph. INS Sujata, an Offshore Patrol Vessel of 103m, is commanded by Commander Jishnu Madhavan, while ICGS Sarathi, an Offshore Patrol Vessel of 105m, is commanded by Commandant Kundan Singh. Meanwhile, the Commanding Officers of the visiting ships called on the Commander Western Naval Area Rear Admiral Harsha De Silva at the Western Naval Command Headquarters today. Mementoes were also exchanged between them, signifying the importance of this occasion. During their stay in the country, the crews and officers under-trainees are scheduled to take part in programmes organised by the Sri Lanka Navy to foster bilateral ties and mutual cooperation. Personnel of the Sri Lanka Navy will also have the opportunity to visit the training operations aboard the vessels and exchange professional expertise. In addition, the visiting personnel are expected to tour several key locations and places of interest across the island during their visit.

content: LAUGFS Gas PLC has officially informed shareholders and the Colombo Stock Exchange that it is engaging in preliminary, informal discussions regarding strategic options for its wholly owned subsidiary, LAUGFS Terminals Limited. LAUGFS Terminals Limited owns and operates a 30,000 MT liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) terminal situated at the Hambantota International Port. In a corporate disclosure submitted to Colombo Stock Exchange today (26) the company confirmed it is holding exploratory talks with interested parties. The options currently under evaluation include commercial collaboration, securing outside investment, or the potential disposal of part or all of LAUGFS Gas PLC’s shareholding in the subsidiary. The company highlighted that no agreement has been reached concerning the structure or terms of any prospective transaction, and no definitive agreement has been executed. LAUGFS Gas PLC noted that there is no assurance these preliminary discussions will result in a finalized deal, meaning any financial impact cannot be determined at present. LAUGFS Gas PLC stated that it will promptly disclose any material developments as required by the Listing Rules of the Colombo Stock Exchange.

summary_en: iDealz Lanka (Pvt) Ltd ආයතනය, iPhone 18 මාදිලිය නිල වශයෙන් වෙළඳපොළට හඳුන්වාදීම පසුගියදා කොළඹදී පැවැත්විය. මෙම අවස්ථාව සඳහා තාක්ෂණික ක්ෂේත්‍රය පිළිබඳව උනන්දුවක් දක්වන්නන්, පාරිභෝගිකයින් ඇතුළු විශාල පිරිසක් එක්ව සිටියහ. මෙම උත්සවයේ ප්‍රධානතම අවස්ථාව වූයේ iPhone 18 මාදිලිය නිල වශයෙන් එළිදැක්වීමයි. නව උපාංග පිළිබඳව විශේෂ අවධානයක් යොමු කෙරුණු මෙම ඉදිරිපත් කිරීමට අමතරව, පාරිභෝගිකයින්ට එම උපාංග සජීවීව පරීක්ෂා කර බැලීම සඳහා විශේෂ අත්දැකීම් කුටියක් ද (Experience Zone) සූදානම් කර තිබිණි. එහිදී උපාංග පෙළ සමීපව නිරීක්ෂණය කිරීමටත්, ප්‍රායෝගික භාවිතය හරහා නිෂ්පාදන පිළිබඳ පැහැදිලි අවබෝධයක් ලබා ගැනීමටත් පැමිණ සිටි පිරිසට අවස්ථාව හිමි විය. එමෙන්ම මෙම එළිදැක්වීම, හුදෙක් නිෂ්පාදනයක් වෙළඳපොළට හඳුන්වා දීමෙන් ඔබ්බට යමින්, පාරිභෝගිකයාට තාක්ෂණය අත්විඳීමටත් නිවැරදි මිලදී ගැනීමේ තීරණ වෙත යොමු වීමටත් අවස්ථාව සලසන නූතන තාක්ෂණික අලෙවිකරණයේ සිදුවෙමින් පවතින පුළුල් වෙනස මනා ලෙස පිළිඹිඹු කළේය. මෙලෙස පාරිභෝගිකයින්ට නව උපාංග සජීවීව අත්විඳීමට පහසුකම් සැලසීම හරහා, නවීන තාක්ෂණය පාරිභෝගිකයාට වඩාත් සමීප කිරීමටත්, සිය සන්නාමය සහ පාරිභෝගිකයා අතර පවතින විශ්වාසනීය සබඳතාව තවදුරටත් ශක්තිමත් කිරීමටත් iDealz දක්වන කැපවීම මනාව පැහැදිලි වේ. iDealz Lanka (Pvt) Ltd හි නිර්මාතෘ සහ සභාපති මොහොමඩ් රිෆ්කාන් මහතා අදහස් දක්වමින් මෙසේ පැව
summary_si: මෙම පුවත Daily FT වෙබ් අඩවියෙන් ලබා ගන්නා ලදී. iDealz Lanka (Pvt) Ltd ආයතනය, iPhone 18 මාදිලිය නිල වශයෙන් වෙළඳපොළට හඳුන්වාදීම පසුගියදා කොළඹදී පැවැත්විය. මෙම අවස්ථාව සඳහා තාක්ෂණික ක්ෂේත්‍රය පිළිබඳව උනන්දුවක් දක්වන්නන්, පාරිභෝගිකයින් ඇතුළු විශාල පිරිසක් එක්ව සිටියහ. මෙම උත්සවයේ ප්‍රධානතම අවස්ථාව වූයේ iPhone 18 මාදිලිය නිල වශයෙන් එළිදැක්වීමයි. නව උපාංග පිළිබඳව විශේෂ අවධානයක් යොමු කෙරුණු මෙම ඉදිරිපත් කිරීමට අමතරව, පාරිභෝගිකයින්ට එම උපාංග සජීවීව පරීක්ෂා කර බැලීම සඳහා විශේෂ අත්දැකීම් කුටියක් ද (Experience Zone) සූදානම් කර තිබිණි. එහිදී උපාංග පෙළ සමීපව නිරීක්ෂණය කිරීමටත්, ප්‍රායෝගික භාවිතය හරහා නිෂ්පාදන පිළිබඳ පැහැදිලි අවබෝධයක් ලබා ගැනීමටත් පැමිණ සිටි පිරිසට අවස්ථාව හිමි විය. එමෙන්ම මෙම එළිදැක්වීම, හුදෙක් නිෂ්පාදනයක් වෙළඳපොළට හඳුන්වා දීමෙන් ඔබ්බට යමින්, පාරිභෝගිකයාට තාක්ෂණය අත්විඳීමටත් නිවැරදි මිලදී ගැනීමේ තීරණ වෙත යොමු වීමටත් අවස්ථාව සලසන නූතන තාක්ෂණික අලෙවිකරණයේ සිදුවෙමින් පවතින පුළුල් වෙනස මනා ලෙස පිළිඹිඹු කළේය. මෙලෙස පාරිභෝගිකයින්ට නව උපාංග සජීවීව අත්විඳීමට පහසුකම් සැලසීම හරහා, නවීන තාක්ෂණය පාරිභෝගිකයාට වඩාත් සමීප කිරීමටත්, සිය සන්නාමය සහ පාරිභෝගිකයා අතර පවතින විශ්වාසනීය සබඳතාව තවදුරටත් ශක්තිමත් කිරීමටත් iDealz දක්වන කැපවීම මනාව පැහැදිලි වේ. iDealz Lanka (Pvt) Ltd හි නිර්මාතෘ සහ සභාපති මොහොමඩ් රිෆ්කාන් මහතා අදහස් දක්වමින් මෙසේ පැව
content: iDealz Lanka (Pvt) Ltd ආයතනය, iPhone 18 මාදිලිය නිල වශයෙන් වෙළඳපොළට හඳුන්වාදීම පසුගියදා කොළඹදී පැවැත්විය. මෙම අවස්ථාව සඳහා තාක්ෂණික ක්ෂේත්‍රය පිළිබඳව උනන්දුවක් දක්වන්නන්, පාරිභෝගිකයින් ඇතුළු විශාල පිරිසක් එක්ව සිටියහ. මෙම උත්සවයේ ප්‍රධානතම අවස්ථාව වූයේ iPhone 18 මාදිලිය නිල වශයෙන් එළිදැක්වීමයි. නව උපාංග පිළිබඳව විශේෂ අවධානයක් යොමු කෙරුණු මෙම ඉදිරිපත් කිරීමට අමතරව, පාරිභෝගිකයින්ට එම උපාංග සජීවීව පරීක්ෂා කර බැලීම සඳහා විශේෂ අත්දැකීම් කුටියක් ද (Experience Zone) සූදානම් කර තිබිණි. එහිදී උපාංග පෙළ සමීපව නිරීක්ෂණය කිරීමටත්, ප්‍රායෝගික භාවිතය හරහා නිෂ්පාදන පිළිබඳ පැහැදිලි අවබෝධයක් ලබා ගැනීමටත් පැමිණ සිටි පිරිසට අවස්ථාව හිමි විය. එමෙන්ම මෙම එළිදැක්වීම, හුදෙක් නිෂ්පාදනයක් වෙළඳපොළට හඳුන්වා දීමෙන් ඔබ්බට යමින්, පාරිභෝගිකයාට තාක්ෂණය අත්විඳීමටත් නිවැරදි මිලදී ගැනීමේ තීරණ වෙත යොමු වීමටත් අවස්ථාව සලසන නූතන තාක්ෂණික අලෙවිකරණයේ සිදුවෙමින් පවතින පුළුල් වෙනස මනා ලෙස පිළිඹිඹු කළේය. මෙලෙස පාරිභෝගිකයින්ට නව උපාංග සජීවීව අත්විඳීමට පහසුකම් සැලසීම හරහා, නවීන තාක්ෂණය පාරිභෝගිකයාට වඩාත් සමීප කිරීමටත්, සිය සන්නාමය සහ පාරිභෝගිකයා අතර පවතින විශ්වාසනීය සබඳතාව තවදුරටත් ශක්තිමත් කිරීමටත් iDealz දක්වන කැපවීම මනාව පැහැදිලි වේ. iDealz Lanka (Pvt) Ltd හි නිර්මාතෘ සහ සභාපති මොහොමඩ් රිෆ්කාන් මහතා අදහස් දක්වමින් මෙසේ පැවසීය. “තාක්ෂණය වඩාත් හොඳින් තේරුම් ගත හැක්කේ පාරිභෝගිකයන්ට එය තමන් විසින්ම සජීවීව අත්විඳීමට අවස්ථාව ලැබුණු විටයි. HELLO18 හරහා අපගේ අරමුණ වූයේ නව උපාංග පෙළක් හඳුන්වාදීමට පමණක් සීමා නොවී, පාරිභෝගිකයන් තාක්ෂණයට තවදුරටත් සමීප කරවන සැබෑ අත්දැකීමක් නිර්මාණය කිරීමයි. මනා දැනුවත්භාවයකින් යුත් මගපෙන්වීම් හරහා සිදුවන අර්ථවත් පාරිභෝගික සන්නිවේදනය, නූතන තාක්ෂණික අලෙවිකරණයේ අත්‍යවශ්‍ය කොටසක් බව අපි විශ්වාස කරනවා.” ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ මොබයිල් සහ තාක්ෂණික අලෙවි ක්ෂේත්‍රය තුළ ස්ථාවර නාමයක් දිනා සිටින iDealz, සිය ප්‍රදර්ශනාගාර සහ ඩිජිටල් නාලිකා හරහා ස්මාර්ට්ෆෝන් සහ ඊට අදාළ උපාංග පාරිභෝගිකයන් වෙත ලබාදීම නිරන්තරයෙන් සිදු කරයි. HELLO18 එළිදැක්වීම මගින් පිළිඹිඹු වන්නේ පාරිභෝගික සන්නිවේදනය කෙරෙහි සමාගම දක්වන නිරන්තර කැපවීම සහ ප්‍රවේශ විය හැකි, දැනුවත්භාවය ලබා දෙන මෙන්ම ආකර්ෂණීය තාක්ෂණික අලෙවිකරණ අත්දැකීමක් ලබා දීමට ඇති අවධානයයි. HELLO18 හරහා අපගේ අරමුණ වූයේ නව උපාංග පෙළක් හඳුන්වාදීමට පමණක් සීමා නොවී, පාරිභෝගිකයන් තාක්ෂණයට තවදුරටත් සමීප කරවන සැබෑ අත්දැකීමක් නිර්මාණය කිරීමයි. මනා දැනුවත්භාවයකින් යුත් මගපෙන්වීම් හරහා සිදුවන අර්ථවත් පාරිභෝගික සන්නිවේදනය, නූතන තාක්ෂණික අලෙවිකරණයේ අත්‍යවශ්‍ය කොටසක් බව අපි විශ්වාස කරනවා.” ශ්‍රී ලංකාවේ මොබයිල් සහ තාක්ෂණික අලෙවි ක්ෂේත්‍රය තුළ ස්ථාවර නාමයක් දිනා සිටින iDealz, සිය ප්‍රදර්ශනාගාර සහ ඩිජිටල් නාලිකා හරහා ස්මාර්ට්ෆෝන් සහ ඊට අදාළ උපාංග පාරිභෝගිකයන් වෙත ලබාදීම නිරන්තරයෙන් සිදු කරයි. Minister orders independent probe into death of man in Homagama Police custody

Public Security and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Ananda Wijepala has instructed Inspector General of Police (IGP) Priyantha Weerasuriya to conduct an urgent and independent investigation into the reported death of a person who was in the custody of the Homagama Police.

The Minister has also instructed the IGP to take further legal action based on the findings of the post-mortem examination and the investigation into the incident.

The Minister emphasised that police officers have a responsibility to ensure the safety of individuals taken into custody and to protect their human dignity.

content: The U.S. Embassy in Sri Lanka appreciates the warm welcome extended to USS Canberra (LCS 30) as the Independence-variant Littoral Combat Ship returns to the Port of Colombo on October 26 for a routine port call. This marks the ship’s second visit to Sri Lanka this year, following a port call in June, and underscores the longstanding partnership between the U.S. and Sri Lankan navies and their shared commitment to maritime security across the Indo-Pacific. “We appreciate the Sri Lanka Navy’s professionalism and support in making these visits smooth and efficient. Each visit reinforces the strength of our naval partnership, built on trust, and our shared commitment to maintaining security and stability across the Indian Ocean,” said U.S. Ambassador to Sri Lanka Eric Meyer.

content: How Sri Lanka Can Turn Great-Power Competition into US$10 Billion in Foreign Investment—and Become the Economic Bridge Between India, China, the Gulf, the USA and West By Jithendra Antonio From Trincomalee’s energy reserves to Colombo’s maritime gateway, from Hambantota’s industrial potential to Mannar’s renewable-energy frontier, Sri Lanka has an opportunity to transform its geography into economic power. The challenge is to attract capital from competing powers without surrendering the freedom to decide its own future. The warning from an Indian Ocean strategist In June 2026, Indian Ocean security entered a fresh round of scrutiny when Keerthi Martyn published “Navigating the Currents: Sri Lanka’s National Security Debate in the New Indian Ocean Order” through the Observer Research Foundation, subsequently republished by the Center for a New American Security. (Link – https://www.orfonline.org/public/uploads/upload/20260623112717.pdf ) Martyn’s assessment raises an uncomfortable question for Colombo – Can Sri Lanka preserve its freedom of action when its location, infrastructure and economic vulnerabilities make it increasingly important to larger powers? The chapter opens with a striking geographical observation. Sri Lanka lies at the crossroads of the Indian Ocean, approximately 10 nautical miles from major sea lanes carrying a substantial share of global energy and container traffic. Martyn argues that this location makes the island both a significant maritime actor and a focus of strategic competition. He identifies intensifying US–China rivalry, China’s infrastructure investments, American maritime-security partnerships and India’s growing influence over Sri Lanka’s security and defence decisions as central pressures shaping the island’s choices. The opening passage also cites a previous article I wrote on January 27, 2025, widely published article, “Sri Lanka’s Maritime Revolution: Must-Do Strategy to Unlock Global Trade Power from Heart of Indian Ocean,” as a reference supporting the strategic significance of Sri Lanka’s location. The citation places the island’s maritime potential within a wider debate about national security and international competition. Martyn’s argument extends beyond geography. His assessment highlights the risks posed by domestic governance weaknesses, limited maritime capabilities, inadequate preparedness for supply-chain disruptions and the difficulty of maintaining strategic flexibility when external powers pursue competing interests. His discussion of the 2026 Iran crisis illustrates how quickly diplomatic choices, maritime incidents and energy vulnerabilities can become interconnected. The Indian Ocean, meanwhile, is not a contest involving only three capitals. It connects India, China, the United States, the Gulf states, Israel and the wider Middle East with Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Bangladesh, Pakistan, the Maldives, East Africa and Europe. Each has different commercial, diplomatic or security interests in the region. The result is a complicated environment in which ports, energy terminals, telecommunications, shipping routes, data infrastructure and investment agreements can acquire significance far beyond their immediate commercial purpose. But there is another way to read the emerging order. What if Sri Lanka stopped treating great-power competition principally as a threat to be managed and began treating it as an economic opportunity to be structured? What if Colombo could attract Indian manufacturing, Chinese industrial investment, American technology, Gulf capital and Israeli innovation under a transparent national framework—while retaining control over its own laws, infrastructure and strategic decisions? That is the economic proposition at the heart of this article. The New Indian Ocean Order does not guarantee Sri Lanka a fortune. It creates an opportunity for the island to earn one. The Ambition – US$10 billion in additional FDI over 20 years Sri Lanka should adopt a national target of attracting US$10 billion in additional realised foreign direct investment between 2027 and 2046 , separate from investment already counted under Colombo Port City. The target is a proposed policy ambition, not an existing government commitment or a forecast of guaranteed investment. The arithmetic is straightforward – US$10 billion over 20 years represents an average of US$500 million annually. The harder task is to attract that money consistently, direct it towards productive sectors and ensure that it generates exports, employment, technology transfer and tax revenue. Sri Lanka has demonstrated that investment on a billion-dollar annual scale is possible, although official figures vary according to whether loans, reinvested earnings and other forms of capital are included. The Central Bank of Sri Lanka and the Board of Investment should therefore establish a common public reporting framework that distinguishes equity capital, intercompany borrowing, reinvested earnings, acquisitions and greenfield investment. The national target should count money actually deployed, not merely memoranda signed or projects announced. It should also measure the results: new export revenue, skilled employment, local supplier participation, wages, technology transfer and the amount of foreign exchange retained in the economy. Sri Lanka needs neither a slogan nor another collection of investment announcements. It needs a pipeline of bankable projects supported by credible institutions. 1. India – Convert Geographic Proximity into an Economic Partnership India deserves its own strategic chapter in Sri Lanka’s investment plan—not because every Indian proposal should automatically be accepted, but because the two countries share a geography that no change in government or international alignment can remove. India is a major economic power, a significant source of Sri Lankan tourism, an important trade partner and a country whose maritime security is closely connected to developments around the island. Its manufacturing base, digital economy, consumer market and energy requirements offer Sri Lanka opportunities that extend well beyond traditional bilateral trade. The High Commission of India in Colombo reports bilateral merchandise trade of approximately US$7.1 billion in financial year 2025–26 and cumulative Indian investment in Sri Lanka of approximately US$2.8 billion, based on Central Bank data. India also became Sri Lanka’s largest source market for tourist arrivals in 2025. These existing connections provide a foundation for further commercial integration. (Source: High Commission of India, Colombo—India–Sri Lanka Economic and Trade Engagement .) The question is how to move from an established relationship towards a more productive economic partnership. A) Build a Sri Lanka–India Manufacturing and Export Corridor Sri Lanka should identify industries in which its workforce, location and existing industrial capabilities can complement India’s much larger market. Potential areas include specialised apparel, rubber-based products, processed food, marine equipment, medical supplies, industrial components and selected engineering services. These are candidates for feasibility studies, not automatic investment winners. The government should create a joint project pipeline that identifies the products India imports competitively, the products Sri Lanka can manufacture efficiently and the markets accessible through regional trade agreements. Projects should be evaluated against landed production costs, rules of origin, electricity prices, shipping expenses and demand from actual buyers. The objective is to make Sri Lanka a complementary production location—not a substitute for the Indian economy. B) Turn Trincomalee into an Energy and Logistics Partnership The Trincomalee energy-hub initiative provides a practical example of how regional economic cooperation can work. In April 2025, Sri Lanka, India and the United Arab Emirates signed a memorandum of understanding to cooperate in developing Trincomalee as an energy hub. The framework includes potential cooperation on the oil-tank farm and associated energy infrastructure. (Source: Announcement by President’s Office of Sri Lanka, 5 April 2025 ) The next phase should identify commercially viable investments in storage, marine fuels, bulk-liquid handling, pipelines, distribution and industrial logistics. A refinery should proceed only if independent analysis establishes a sustainable business case, including feedstock availability, market demand, financing costs and environmental compliance. C) Connect the Electricity Systems A high-voltage direct-current interconnection between India and Sri Lanka could eventually enable electricity exchange and improve the commercial utilisation of renewable power, subject to final engineering, regulatory and financing arrangements. The two governments exchanged an understanding on electricity interconnection in April 2025. India’s official briefing described the initiative as a way to support lower-cost electricity and potentially enable Sri Lanka to export clean energy. (Source: High Commission of India—April 2025 briefing .) Sri Lanka should prepare its generation, transmission and regulatory systems so that it can benefit from such connectivity rather than simply becoming a passive electricity purchaser. D) Develop Digital and Professional Services The island can serve businesses that need regional expertise, multilingual customer support, software development, accounting, engineering, compliance, logistics management and other internationally tradable services. A joint programme with Indian companies and universities could establish specialised training centres, digital-service operations and export-oriented technology businesses. This is an area in which Sri Lanka can benefit from Indian economic growth without attempting to replicate the entire scale of India’s technology industry. The larger Strategic Dividend A more prosperous and economically connected neighbourhood can create opportunities for Sri Lanka to strengthen its maritime services, energy links and industrial capabilities. The concept sometimes described as Pax India —an Indian Ocean environment in which India’s economic scale and regional relationships contribute to stability and connectivity—should be treated as a possible strategic framework, not an established doctrine or a guarantee of Indian support. Sri Lanka’s interest is to make the relationship commercially valuable to both countries while preserving its sovereign right to negotiate the terms of every project. The strongest partnership is not one in which Colombo depends on New Delhi to solve every economic problem. It is one in which both countries benefit from a more productive, connected and stable region. 2. China – Welcome Industrial Capital, But Make Every Project Earn its Place China remains a major participant in Sri Lanka’s infrastructure and industrial development. Its construction capabilities, manufacturing ecosystem, financing networks and experience in large-scale industrial projects make it an important potential investor. Yet the economic question is not whether a project is Chinese or Indian. It is whether the project generates sufficient value for Sri Lanka. That distinction matters because infrastructure can become an asset or a liability depending on the terms of financing, the level of utilisation, the allocation of risk and the revenue it produces. Sri Lanka should pursue a more sophisticated relationship with Chinese capital: one that welcomes viable investments while insisting on transparent contracts, sound financing, environmental safeguards and measurable economic outcomes. A) Hambantota – Build an Industrial Economy around the Port In January 2025, the Sri Lankan Embassy in Beijing announced an agreement with Sinopec for a proposed US$3.7 billion refinery in the Hambantota region, with a stated processing capacity of 200,000 barrels per day and a substantial export orientation. Source: Embassy of Sri Lanka in Beijing, 16 January 2025 . The announcement represents a substantial industrial ambition. Its ultimate contribution will depend on implementation, financing, feedstock arrangements, market demand, environmental performance and the terms governing the investment. A refinery should not be evaluated solely by its headline value. The relevant questions are whether it will generate net foreign exchange, whether its output can be sold competitively, whether Sri Lankan workers and suppliers will participate and whether public finances are protected from unanticipated liabilities. The wider opportunity is to create an industrial ecosystem around Hambantota that can support warehousing, port services, industrial maintenance, packaging, engineering, export manufacturing and logistics. If a refinery proceeds, it should become an anchor for commercially viable activity—not an isolated project surrounded by empty industrial land. B) Industrial Parks and Export Manufacturing Chinese companies could be invited to develop or participate in export-oriented manufacturing projects in sectors such as industrial components, machinery, electronics assembly, rubber products and selected consumer goods. Sri Lanka should not compete for factories simply by offering cheap land or tax concessions. It should compete by reducing the total cost of producing and exporting goods. That means reliable electricity, efficient customs, good transport links, skilled workers and predictable regulations. Investment agreements should specify employment targets where appropriate, environmental obligations, local-supplier opportunities and transparent reporting. C) Maritime Technology and Port Operations China’s expertise in port construction, logistics systems and industrial infrastructure may support selected projects in port management, cargo handling, warehousing and digital logistics. However, projects involving critical infrastructure require appropriate cybersecurity, data-protection and national-security assessments. Sri Lanka should retain the ability to inspect, regulate and protect essential systems. D) Renewable Energy and Industrial Technology Chinese companies are major participants in global solar, battery and electric-vehicle supply chains. Sri Lanka could invite competitive proposals for renewable-energy equipment, storage, grid technology and export-oriented manufacturing where local conditions justify the investment. Procurement should be open to qualified suppliers from different countries, with decisions based on lifecycle cost, reliability, financing and technical performance. The Principle China should remain an economic partner, but not an economic exception. No foreign investor should receive favourable treatment that cannot be justified under a transparent national framework. No project should be described as a success merely because it carries a multibillion-dollar price tag. The real test is whether Sri Lanka becomes more productive, more export-capable and less vulnerable after the investment. 3. The United States – Turn Maritime Security into a Wider Commercial Relationship The United States has a significant interest in freedom of navigation, regional stability, maritime awareness and the resilience of international supply chains. These interests overlap with Sri Lanka’s need for safe shipping routes, reliable infrastructure and a more diversified export economy. But the relationship should extend beyond naval cooperation and diplomatic engagement. Sri Lanka should make itself more attractive to American businesses seeking skilled workers, regional access, reliable digital infrastructure and an export-oriented operating base. A) Digital Services and Technology Potential investment areas include software engineering, cloud services, business-process operations, cybersecurity, financial technology, data infrastructure and specialised professional services. These businesses can generate foreign exchange without requiring every investment to take the form of a large physical industrial complex. The conditions for attracting them are practical: dependable electricity, robust connectivity, data-protection rules, intellectual-property safeguards, professional skills and predictable regulation. B) Maritime Logistics and Supply-Chain Services Sri Lanka can explore commercial partnerships involving vessel services, cargo visibility, logistics software, shipping support and supply-chain management. A modern port is not merely a place where containers are lifted from ships. It is a node in a global information network. The country should invest in interoperable cargo documentation, modern customs systems, vessel scheduling and reliable data exchange. Those improvements can make Sri Lanka more useful to shipping companies and manufacturers across multiple countries. C) Advanced Manufacturing and Agricultural Technology American firms could participate in selected projects involving medical technology, specialised manufacturing, food processing, agricultural technology and industrial automation. The government should target companies with a clear commercial rationale for locating in Sri Lanka and assess each proposal on its own merits. D) Maritime Resilience and Disaster Preparedness Maritime surveillance, search and rescue, disaster response and supply-chain resilience are areas where international cooperation can support national capacity. Sri Lanka should pursue partnerships that improve its ability to protect its waters, respond to emergencies and maintain essential imports during crises. Security cooperation should strengthen the country’s own institutions and capabilities, not create unnecessary dependence on any single external partner. The Commercial Objective The United States should be one of several major sources of investment and technology for Sri Lanka. The island should not expect Washington to finance its entire development strategy, nor should it allow geopolitical disagreements to prevent commercially valuable cooperation. A predictable business environment is the most persuasive investment promotion campaign Sri Lanka can conduct. 4. The seven Gulf states – Connect Capital with Energy, Logistics and Global Markets The Gulf should be treated as a diverse investment region rather than a single pool of oil money. The seven states most relevant to a wider Sri Lankan Gulf investment strategy are the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman, and Bahrain . The six are members of the Gulf Cooperation Council. Their investment capabilities differ. Sri Lanka should approach each according to its financial institutions, energy sector, logistics networks, industrial priorities and appetite for overseas investment. A) United Arab Emirates – Logistics, Ports and International Business The UAE is a natural candidate for investment in logistics, port-linked services, energy infrastructure, warehousing, tourism and international business operations. Its experience in maritime logistics and global connectivity could be particularly relevant to Colombo, Hambantota and Trincomalee. The trilateral Trincomalee energy-hub memorandum involving Sri Lanka, India and the UAE already provides an institutional starting point for further commercial work. Sri Lanka should seek investment proposals with clearly defined ownership, financing, operational responsibilities and expected revenue. It should also examine opportunities in cold-chain logistics, aviation-linked tourism, maritime services and regional distribution. B) Saudi Arabia – Energy, Industry and Tourism Saudi Arabia’s economic diversification programme creates potential opportunities beyond conventional petroleum investment. Sri Lanka could explore renewable energy, energy storage, tourism infrastructure, industrial services, food processing and selected logistics projects. The priority should be to identify projects that fit the commercial objectives of Saudi investors while creating durable economic activity in Sri Lanka. Large tourism developments, for example, should be supported by independent assessments of demand, water use, environmental impact and infrastructure capacity. C) Qatar – Energy, Finance and Aviation Connectivity Qatar’s strengths in energy, aviation, investment and international business create potential for partnerships in logistics, energy infrastructure, hospitality and financial services. Sri Lanka should explore commercially viable investment and co-financing opportunities, including projects that improve connectivity between the island and major international markets. The focus should be on projects that produce measurable income and employment rather than relying on broad diplomatic statements about future cooperation. D) Kuwait – Institutional Capital and Infrastructure Kuwait offers a potential source of investment through financial institutions, investment vehicles and private businesses. Sri Lanka should prepare professionally assessed opportunities in infrastructure, energy, property development and export-oriented industries. Projects should have clear revenue models and transparent risk allocation. Where public guarantees are requested, their fiscal cost should be disclosed. E) Oman – Maritime Services, Energy and Logistics Oman’s position along important maritime routes and its experience in ports, logistics and energy provide a potential basis for cooperation. Sri Lanka could explore port services, shipping support, marine maintenance, fuel logistics and selected renewable-energy projects. The two countries could also examine opportunities in maritime training and technical services. F) Bahrain – Financial Services and Fintech Bahrain’s financial-services sector provides a potential partner for Sri Lanka’s ambition to develop international business, financial technology, compliance and professional services. Any such initiative should depend on credible regulation, appropriate anti-money-laundering safeguards, investor protection and the ability to serve genuine commercial customers. Sri Lanka should not pursue a financial-services strategy based on regulatory shortcuts. Its competitive advantage must be trust. One Gulf strategy, Six Differentiated Approaches Sri Lanka should establish a Gulf Investment Programme that identifies specific investors, project requirements, financing conditions and implementation timelines. It should not assume that every Gulf state has the same investment capacity or priorities. Nor should it confuse memoranda of understanding with money committed. The programme should be supported by a professional project-preparation team capable of presenting bankable proposals in energy, logistics, manufacturing, tourism and services. The goal is to convert diplomatic relationships into transactions that survive commercial due diligence. 5. Israel – Technology Partnerships in Water, Agriculture and Resilience Israel offers a distinct set of potential partnerships in specialised technology, particularly in water management, irrigation, precision agriculture, cybersecurity and selected medical technologies. Sri Lanka faces practical challenges involving agricultural productivity, water efficiency, climate resilience and the protection of digital infrastructure. Technology partnerships could help address these issues if the solutions are adapted to local conditions. A) Water and Agricultural Productivity Potential projects include precision irrigation, soil monitoring, greenhouse technology, water treatment and systems that improve crop yields while reducing resource use. Sri Lanka should begin with pilot projects and independent evaluations rather than assume that a technology developed for one environment will automatically work in another. Successful pilots could then be scaled through transparent procurement and partnerships with local agricultural institutions. B) Food Processing and Agricultural Exports Improved agricultural technology could be linked to cold-chain logistics, food processing, quality assurance and export certification. The aim should be to increase the value earned by Sri Lankan producers, not merely to import more equipment. C) Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure As Sri Lanka digitises ports, energy systems, financial services and public administration, the need for robust cybersecurity will grow. Specialist international providers, including Israeli firms, could compete to deliver security systems, training and risk-management services. Such projects should be subject to clear rules governing data ownership, access, system integrity and national oversight. D) Medical and Specialised Technology Sri Lanka could also explore partnerships in selected medical technologies and healthcare services where there is a demonstrable clinical and commercial case. The objective should be better services, local skills and sustainable costs—not technology imports for their own sake. Israel should be one of several international technology partners. Commercial decisions should follow transparent procurement, national law and an assessment of each project’s benefits and risks. 6. The wider Indian Ocean – Singapore, Japan, South Korea and the ASEAN Economies A strategy focused only on India, China, the United States, the Gulf and Israel would miss other valuable sources of expertise and capital. Singapore has extensive experience in port operations, trade facilitation, financial services and regional business management. Sri Lanka could work with Singaporean companies to improve logistics, professional services and internationally tradable business operations. Japan and South Korea could contribute to industrial technology, transport, energy systems, advanced manufacturing and workforce development. Australia could be a partner in education, maritime cooperation, tourism and selected resource and technology projects. Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand offer opportunities in food processing, manufacturing, tourism and regional trade. The European economies can contribute to renewable energy, advanced manufacturing, sustainable infrastructure, professional services and technology. These relationships should be treated as complements to, not replacements for, the larger investment partnerships described above. The strategic advantage of Sri Lanka is not that it must choose a single centre of economic gravity. It is that the island can connect several markets if its institutions and infrastructure are sufficiently reliable. 7. passive_voice_content: How Sri Lanka Can Turn Great-Power Competition into US$10 Billion in Foreign Investment—and Become the Economic Bridge Between India, China, the Gulf, the USA and West By Jithendra Antonio From Trincomalee’s energy reserves to Colombo’s maritime gateway, from Hambantota’s industrial potential to Mannar’s renewable-energy frontier, Sri Lanka has an opportunity to transform its geography into economic power. The challenge is to attract capital from competing powers without surrendering the freedom to decide its own future. The warning from an Indian Ocean strategist In June 2026, Indian Ocean security entered a fresh round of scrutiny when Keerthi Martyn published “Navigating the Currents: Sri Lanka’s National Security Debate in the New Indian Ocean Order” through the Observer Research Foundation, subsequently republished by the Center for a New American Security. (Link – https://www.orfonline.org/public/uploads/upload/20260623112717.pdf ) Martyn’s assessment raises an uncomfortable question for Colombo – Can Sri Lanka preserve its freedom of action when its location, infrastructure and economic vulnerabilities make it increasingly important to larger powers? The chapter opens with a striking geographical observation. Sri Lanka lies at the crossroads of the Indian Ocean, approximately 10 nautical miles from major sea lanes carrying a substantial share of global energy and container traffic. Martyn argues that this location makes the island both a significant maritime actor and a focus of strategic competition. He identifies intensifying US–China rivalry, China’s infrastructure investments, American maritime-security partnerships and India’s growing influence over Sri Lanka’s security and defence decisions as central pressures shaping the island’s choices. The opening passage also cites a previous article I wrote on January 27, 2025, widely published article, “Sri Lanka’s Maritime Revolution: Must-Do Strategy to Unlock Global Trade Power from Heart of Indian Ocean,” as a reference supporting the strategic significance of Sri Lanka’s location. The citation places the island’s maritime potential within a wider debate about national security and international competition. Martyn’s argument extends beyond geography. His assessment highlights the risks posed by domestic governance weaknesses, limited maritime capabilities, inadequate preparedness for supply-chain disruptions and the difficulty of maintaining strategic flexibility when external powers pursue competing interests. His discussion of the 2026 Iran crisis illustrates how quickly diplomatic choices, maritime incidents and energy vulnerabilities can become interconnected. The Indian Ocean, meanwhile, is not a contest involving only three capitals. It connects India, China, the United States, the Gulf states, Israel and the wider Middle East with Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Bangladesh, Pakistan, the Maldives, East Africa and Europe. Each has different commercial, diplomatic or security interests in the region. The result is a complicated environment in which ports, energy terminals, telecommunications, shipping routes, data infrastructure and investment agreements can acquire significance far beyond their immediate commercial purpose. But there is another way to read the emerging order. What if Sri Lanka stopped treating great-power competition principally as a threat to be managed and began treating it as an economic opportunity to be structured? What if Colombo could attract Indian manufacturing, Chinese industrial investment, American technology, Gulf capital and Israeli innovation under a transparent national framework—while retaining control over its own laws, infrastructure and strategic decisions? That is the economic proposition at the heart of this article. The New Indian Ocean Order does not guarantee Sri Lanka a fortune. It creates an opportunity for the island to earn one. The Ambition – US$10 billion in additional FDI over 20 years Sri Lanka should adopt a national target of attracting US$10 billion in additional realised foreign direct investment between 2027 and 2046 , separate from investment already counted under Colombo Port City. The target is a proposed policy ambition, not an existing government commitment or a forecast of guaranteed investment. The arithmetic is straightforward – US$10 billion over 20 years represents an average of US$500 million annually. The harder task is to attract that money consistently, direct it towards productive sectors and ensure that it generates exports, employment, technology transfer and tax revenue. Sri Lanka has demonstrated that investment on a billion-dollar annual scale is possible, although official figures vary according to whether loans, reinvested earnings and other forms of capital are included. The Central Bank of Sri Lanka and the Board of Investment should therefore establish a common public reporting framework that distinguishes equity capital, intercompany borrowing, reinvested earnings, acquisitions and greenfield investment. The national target should count money actually deployed, not merely memoranda signed or projects announced. It should also measure the results: new export revenue, skilled employment, local supplier participation, wages, technology transfer and the amount of foreign exchange retained in the economy. Sri Lanka needs neither a slogan nor another collection of investment announcements. It needs a pipeline of bankable projects supported by credible institutions. 1. India – Convert Geographic Proximity into an Economic Partnership India deserves its own strategic chapter in Sri Lanka’s investment plan—not because every Indian proposal should automatically be accepted, but because the two countries share a geography that no change in government or international alignment can remove. India is a major economic power, a significant source of Sri Lankan tourism, an important trade partner and a country whose maritime security is closely connected to developments around the island. Its manufacturing base, digital economy, consumer market and energy requirements offer Sri Lanka opportunities that extend well beyond traditional bilateral trade. The High Commission of India in Colombo reports bilateral merchandise trade of approximately US$7.1 billion in financial year 2025–26 and cumulative Indian investment in Sri Lanka of approximately US$2.8 billion, based on Central Bank data. India also became Sri Lanka’s largest source market for tourist arrivals in 2025. These existing connections provide a foundation for further commercial integration. (Source: High Commission of India, Colombo—India–Sri Lanka Economic and Trade Engagement .) The question is how to move from an established relationship towards a more productive economic partnership. A) Build a Sri Lanka–India Manufacturing and Export Corridor Sri Lanka should identify industries in which its workforce, location and existing industrial capabilities can complement India’s much larger market. Potential areas include specialised apparel, rubber-based products, processed food, marine equipment, medical supplies, industrial components and selected engineering services. These are candidates for feasibility studies, not automatic investment winners. The government should create a joint project pipeline that identifies the products India imports competitively, the products Sri Lanka can manufacture efficiently and the markets accessible through regional trade agreements. Projects should be evaluated against landed production costs, rules of origin, electricity prices, shipping expenses and demand from actual buyers. The objective is to make Sri Lanka a complementary production location—not a substitute for the Indian economy. B) Turn Trincomalee into an Energy and Logistics Partnership The Trincomalee energy-hub initiative provides a practical example of how regional economic cooperation can work. In April 2025, Sri Lanka, India and the United Arab Emirates signed a memorandum of understanding to cooperate in developing Trincomalee as an energy hub. The framework includes potential cooperation on the oil-tank farm and associated energy infrastructure. (Source: Announcement by President’s Office of Sri Lanka, 5 April 2025 ) The next phase should identify commercially viable investments in storage, marine fuels, bulk-liquid handling, pipelines, distribution and industrial logistics. A refinery should proceed only if independent analysis establishes a sustainable business case, including feedstock availability, market demand, financing costs and environmental compliance. C) Connect the Electricity Systems A high-voltage direct-current interconnection between India and Sri Lanka could eventually enable electricity exchange and improve the commercial utilisation of renewable power, subject to final engineering, regulatory and financing arrangements. The two governments exchanged an understanding on electricity interconnection in April 2025. India’s official briefing described the initiative as a way to support lower-cost electricity and potentially enable Sri Lanka to export clean energy. (Source: High Commission of India—April 2025 briefing .) Sri Lanka should prepare its generation, transmission and regulatory systems so that it can benefit from such connectivity rather than simply becoming a passive electricity purchaser. D) Develop Digital and Professional Services The island can serve businesses that need regional expertise, multilingual customer support, software development, accounting, engineering, compliance, logistics management and other internationally tradable services. A joint programme with Indian companies and universities could establish specialised training centres, digital-service operations and export-oriented technology businesses. This is an area in which Sri Lanka can benefit from Indian economic growth without attempting to replicate the entire scale of India’s technology industry. The larger Strategic Dividend A more prosperous and economically connected neighbourhood can create opportunities for Sri Lanka to strengthen its maritime services, energy links and industrial capabilities. The concept sometimes described as Pax India —an Indian Ocean environment in which India’s economic scale and regional relationships contribute to stability and connectivity—should be treated as a possible strategic framework, not an established doctrine or a guarantee of Indian support. Sri Lanka’s interest is to make the relationship commercially valuable to both countries while preserving its sovereign right to negotiate the terms of every project. The strongest partnership is not one in which Colombo depends on New Delhi to solve every economic problem. It is one in which both countries benefit from a more productive, connected and stable region. 2. Its construction capabilities, manufacturing ecosystem, financing networks and experience in large-scale industrial projects make it an important potential investor. Yet the economic question is not whether a project is Chinese or Indian. It is whether the project generates sufficient value for Sri Lanka. That distinction matters because infrastructure can become an asset or a liability depending on the terms of financing, the level of utilisation, the allocation of risk and the revenue it produces. Sri Lanka should pursue a more sophisticated relationship with Chinese capital: one that welcomes viable investments while insisting on transparent contracts, sound financing, environmental safeguards and measurable economic outcomes. A) Hambantota – Build an Industrial Economy around the Port In January 2025, the Sri Lankan Embassy in Beijing announced an agreement with Sinopec for a proposed US$3.7 billion refinery in the Hambantota region, with a stated processing capacity of 200,000 barrels per day and a substantial export orientation. Source: Embassy of Sri Lanka in Beijing, 16 January 2025 . The announcement represents a substantial industrial ambition. Its ultimate contribution will depend on implementation, financing, feedstock arrangements, market demand, environmental performance and the terms governing the investment. A refinery should not be evaluated solely by its headline value. The relevant questions are whether it will generate net foreign exchange, whether its output can be sold competitively, whether Sri Lankan workers and suppliers will participate and whether public finances are protected from unanticipated liabilities. The wider opportunity is to create an industrial ecosystem around Hambantota that can support warehousing, port services, industrial maintenance, packaging, engineering, export manufacturing and logistics. If a refinery proceeds, it should become an anchor for commercially viable activity—not an isolated project surrounded by empty industrial land. B) Industrial Parks and Export Manufacturing Chinese companies could be invited to develop or participate in export-oriented manufacturing projects in sectors such as industrial components, machinery, electronics assembly, rubber products and selected consumer goods. Sri Lanka should not compete for factories simply by offering cheap land or tax concessions. It should compete by reducing the total cost of producing and exporting goods. That means reliable electricity, efficient customs, good transport links, skilled workers and predictable regulations. Investment agreements should specify employment targets where appropriate, environmental obligations, local-supplier opportunities and transparent reporting. C) Maritime Technology and Port Operations China’s expertise in port construction, logistics systems and industrial infrastructure may support selected projects in port management, cargo handling, warehousing and digital logistics. However, projects involving critical infrastructure require appropriate cybersecurity, data-protection and national-security assessments. Sri Lanka should retain the ability to inspect, regulate and protect essential systems. D) Renewable Energy and Industrial Technology Chinese companies are major participants in global solar, battery and electric-vehicle supply chains. Sri Lanka could invite competitive proposals for renewable-energy equipment, storage, grid technology and export-oriented manufacturing where local conditions justify the investment. Procurement should be open to qualified suppliers from different countries, with decisions based on lifecycle cost, reliability, financing and technical performance. These businesses can generate foreign exchange without requiring every investment to take the form of a large physical industrial complex. The conditions for attracting them are practical: dependable electricity, robust connectivity, data-protection rules, intellectual-property safeguards, professional skills and predictable regulation. A modern port is not merely a place where containers are lifted from ships. It is a node in a global information network. The country should invest in interoperable cargo documentation, modern customs systems, vessel scheduling and reliable data exchange. Those improvements can make Sri Lanka more useful to shipping companies and manufacturers across multiple countries. C) Advanced Manufacturing and Agricultural Technology American firms could participate in selected projects involving medical technology, specialised manufacturing, food processing, agricultural technology and industrial automation. The government should target companies with a clear commercial rationale for locating in Sri Lanka and assess each proposal on its own merits. D) Maritime Resilience and Disaster Preparedness Maritime surveillance, search and rescue, disaster response and supply-chain resilience are areas where international cooperation can support national capacity. Sri Lanka should pursue partnerships that improve its ability to protect its waters, respond to emergencies and maintain essential imports during crises. Security cooperation should strengthen the country’s own institutions and capabilities, not create unnecessary dependence on any single external partner. A predictable business environment is the most persuasive investment promotion campaign Sri Lanka can conduct. 4. It should also examine opportunities in cold-chain logistics, aviation-linked tourism, maritime services and regional distribution. B) Saudi Arabia – Energy, Industry and Tourism Saudi Arabia’s economic diversification programme creates potential opportunities beyond conventional petroleum investment. Sri Lanka could explore renewable energy, energy storage, tourism infrastructure, industrial services, food processing and selected logistics projects. The priority should be to identify projects that fit the commercial objectives of Saudi investors while creating durable economic activity in Sri Lanka. Large tourism developments, for example, should be supported by independent assessments of demand, water use, environmental impact and infrastructure capacity. C) Qatar – Energy, Finance and Aviation Connectivity Qatar’s strengths in energy, aviation, investment and international business create potential for partnerships in logistics, energy infrastructure, hospitality and financial services. Sri Lanka should explore commercially viable investment and co-financing opportunities, including projects that improve connectivity between the island and major international markets. The goal is to convert diplomatic relationships into transactions that survive commercial due diligence. 5. Successful pilots could then be scaled through transparent procurement and partnerships with local agricultural institutions. content: The United States Navy ship USS Canberra (LCS-30) arrived at the Port of Colombo this morning, 26 October 2026 for replenishment purposes. The visiting ship was welcomed by the Sri Lanka Navy in accordance with naval traditions. This 127.6 metre long Littoral Combat Ship (LCS) is commanded by Commander C Towles. Commissioned on 22 July 2023, USS Canberra (LCS-30) has since been in service with the US Navy. The ship previously made a port call in Sri Lanka on 12 June this year.

content:
Grammy-winning singer Chris Brown is to be sentenced Monday over brawling at a London nightclub three years ago.

Brown, 37, pleaded guilty to a count of affray at London’s Southwark Crown Court in July for attacking a music producer with a bottle on the head.

Brown had denied attacking Abraham Diaw with a bottle at the Tape nightclub in the swanky Mayfair neighborhood in February 2023. But prosecutors said the fight was caught on surveillance camera in front of a club full of people.

In return for the guilty plea, prosecutors dropped charges of assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm and having an offensive weapon, a bottle.

Brown's friend and vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu also pleaded guilty to affray. He will be sentenced too.

Brown left the United Kingdom after the brawl but was arrested in May 2025 at a Manchester hotel after flying to the city for a concert.

Brown had been free on bail of 5 million pounds ($6.7 million), which allowed him to tour Europe and North America last summer. He was freed on bail again Friday and will be sentenced Oct. 26 on the affray charge, which carries a maximum sentence of three years in prison.

Brown, who rose to stardom as a teen in 2005, won his first Grammy for best R&B album in 2011 for “F.A.M.E.” He earned his second in the same category for “11:11 (Deluxe)” in 2025.

He has been in repeated legal trouble since his felony conviction in the 2009 assault of his then-girlfriend, Rihanna, hours before the pair were due to perform at the Grammys.

He has been arrested in several U.S. states over altercations, and in 2019 he was arrested in Paris and questioned on suspicion of rape. He was released without charge.

Brown had denied attacking Abraham Diaw with a bottle at the Tape nightclub in the swanky Mayfair neighborhood in February 2023. But prosecutors said the fight was caught on surveillance camera in front of a club full of people.

In return for the guilty plea, prosecutors dropped charges of assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm and having an offensive weapon, a bottle.

Brown's friend and vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu also pleaded guilty to affray. He will be sentenced too.

Brown left the United Kingdom after the brawl but was arrested in May 2025 at a Manchester hotel after flying to the city for a concert.

Brown had been free on bail of 5 million pounds ($6.7 million), which allowed him to tour Europe and North America last summer. He was freed on bail again Friday and will be sentenced Oct. 26 on the affray charge, which carries a maximum sentence of three years in prison.

Brown, who rose to stardom as a teen in 2005, won his first Grammy for best R&B album in 2011 for “F.A.M.E.” He earned his second in the same category for “11:11 (Deluxe)” in 2025.

He has been in repeated legal trouble since his felony conviction in the 2009 assault of his then-girlfriend, Rihanna, hours before the pair were due to perform at the Grammys.

He has been arrested in several U.S. states over altercations, and in 2019 he was arrested in Paris and questioned on suspicion of rape. He was released without charge.
